title: Memory leak after a bad deploy (OOMKilled pods)
steps: Step 1: Check whether OOMKilled restarts began right after the latest deploy (kubectl rollout history, ArgoCD sync time).
Step 2: Confirm memory grows steadily per pod (about 10 MB/min or more) rather than spiking with traffic.
Step 3: Do NOT rely on restarts or raising memory limits. They only delay the crash by 20-30 minutes.
Step 4: Roll back to the previous release: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<service> or revert the ArgoCD revision.
Step 5: Verify memory working set stays flat for 15 minutes and 5xx rate returns to baseline.
Step 6: Open a ticket with the release owner and attach a heap dump if one was captured.

title: Postgres connection pool exhaustion
steps: Step 1: Check pgbouncer stats (SHOW POOLS): cl_waiting above 50 with sv_active at pool_size means exhaustion.
Step 2: Check whether nightly-settlement-batch (or any batch job) is running and holding many connections.
Step 3: Do NOT scale up application pods or raise max_connections. This adds more clients to the same saturated pool and has failed in every past incident.
Step 4: Pause the batch: kubectl patch cronjob nightly-settlement-batch -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' and delete the running job.
Step 5: Restart pgbouncer: kubectl rollout restart deployment/pgbouncer.
Step 6: Confirm cl_waiting drops to 0 and API latency recovers, then resume the batch only in the off-peak window.

title: Redis primary failover (self-hosted Redis)
reason: We migrated to managed Redis, so manual failover steps no longer apply.
steps: Step 1: Check sentinel state: redis-cli -h redis-sentinel -p 26379 SENTINEL master mymaster.
Step 2: If no automatic promotion occurred, force it: SENTINEL failover mymaster.
Step 3: Confirm the new master with SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name mymaster.
Step 4: Rolling restart checkout-service so clients drop the cached old master address.
Step 5: Investigate why the old master failed (memory, node, network) before bringing it back as a replica.

title: Expired or failing TLS certificate renewal
steps: Step 1: Identify the expired certificate: kubectl get certificate -A and check notAfter, or inspect it with openssl s_client.
Step 2: Check cert-manager: kubectl describe certificate and challenges, and confirm the issuer's renewal job is not suspended.
Step 3: Do NOT just restart pods or ingress. They reload the same expired certificate.
Step 4: Fix the cause (ACME challenge path blocked, suspended renewal, manually managed secret) then force renewal: cmctl renew <certificate>.
Step 5: Roll affected pods so they load the new certificate and verify with openssl s_client.
Step 6: Make sure expiry alerts at 14 days exist for this certificate.

title: Disk full on Postgres volume or Kubernetes node
steps: Step 1: Find what is consuming space: df -h, du on the volume, and pg_wal size for Postgres.
Step 2: For Postgres, check pg_replication_slots for inactive slots retaining WAL and drop abandoned ones.
Step 3: For nodes, check container logs (debug logging left on) and unused images: crictl rmi --prune.
Step 4: Do NOT delete evicted pods or restart log shippers. These do not free space.
Step 5: If space is still short, expand the PVC or add node storage.
Step 6: Add or tune alerts (replication slot lag, node filesystem at 80%).

title: DNS resolution failures (CoreDNS)
steps: Step 1: Check CoreDNS pods: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns for CrashLoopBackOff or missing replicas.
Step 2: If pods crash, read their logs for Corefile errors and revert the ConfigMap to the previous revision.
Step 3: If pods are healthy but throttled or too few, scale coredns to at least 4 replicas.
Step 4: Do NOT restart application pods. They are not the cause.
Step 5: Verify with nslookup from a debug pod and watch the error rate return to zero.

title: Upstream API rate limiting (429 responses)
steps: Step 1: Compare outbound requests per minute with the vendor's documented quota.
Step 2: Reduce call volume: enable request batching or caching, and lower retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
Step 3: Do NOT raise retry counts or replay dead-letter queues while throttled. This amplifies the problem.
Step 4: Contact the vendor for a temporary quota increase if traffic is legitimate.
Step 5: Drain the manual review or dead-letter queue slowly once error rates are normal.

title: Managed Redis failover
steps: Step 1: Do NOT use sentinel commands. The managed service has no sentinels to command (that was RB-12).
Step 2: Open the managed Redis console and confirm which node is the current primary and the failover event time.
Step 3: If no automatic failover occurred, trigger one from the managed Redis control-plane (console or CLI).
Step 4: Roll checkout-service pods so clients re-resolve the managed endpoint DNS and drop the old primary address.
Step 5: Verify cart writes succeed and READONLY errors stop.
Step 6: Record the provider maintenance or failover reason in the incident.
